1a.fix: Slide 14 prints 4\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, which is not balanced (8 Cu and 4 S on the left, 4 Cu and 2 S on the right). The balanced reaction is 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}.
1a.html:
Roasting is the heating of an ore or concentrate below its fusion point, usually in excess air, to bring about a chemical change that converts it into a form more suitable for the next step of extraction: reduction (smelting) or leaching. The charge stays solid throughout. Roasting precedes smelting in pyrometallurgy and leaching in hydrometallurgy.

Why it is needed. Most non-ferrous metals occur as sulphides, and carbon cannot reduce a sulphide because the free energy change is positive:

2\,\mathrm{ZnS} + \mathrm{C} = 2\,\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{CS_2}, \qquad \Delta G^\circ = +105\ \mathrm{kcal\ at\ 0^\circ C},\ +60\ \mathrm{kcal\ at\ 900^\circ C}

Sulphides are also insoluble in water, so they leach poorly. An oxide is reduced far more easily, and an oxide or sulphate leaches easily.

Principal object. The principal object of most roasting operations is to oxidise the sulphide particles to oxides or sulphates without fusing the charge. The particles are exposed to a current of air and ignited, and the air carries the \mathrm{SO_2} away:

2\,\mathrm{ZnS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{ZnO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
4\,\mathrm{FeS_2} + 11\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\,\mathrm{SO_2}
\mathrm{MS} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{MSO_4}\quad \text{(sulphate, for leaching)}

When almost all the sulphur is removed the product is a dead roast; a partial roast leaves enough sulphur to form a matte.

Other objects: to volatilise impurities such as As and Sb as \mathrm{As_2O_3} and \mathrm{Sb_2O_3}, and to convert the charge into a porous sinter (agglomerate) for the blast furnace.
pts: Defines roasting as heating an ore or concentrate below its fusion point, in excess air, so the charge stays solid
States the aim of the conversion: a form suitable for subsequent reduction (smelting) or leaching

Explains why sulphides are roasted: carbon cannot reduce them (\Delta G^\circ positive, for example 2\mathrm{ZnS} + \mathrm{C}) and they are insoluble, while oxides reduce and oxides or sulphates leach easily
Principal object: to oxidise the sulphide particles to oxides or sulphates without fusing the charge, with \mathrm{SO_2} carried away by the air

Gives at least one balanced roasting reaction, for example 2\mathrm{ZnS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{ZnO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} or 4\mathrm{FeS_2} + 11\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\mathrm{SO_2}
Names a further object (volatilising As or Sb, sintering the charge) or defines a dead roast
1a.watch:
• "Principal object" has a one-line answer (oxidise sulphides to oxides or sulphates); state it as a sentence, not only as a reaction.
  • Do not say the charge melts: fusion would seal the particles and stop the gas reaching them. Smelting, not roasting, melts the charge.
  • Balance the pyrite reaction: 4 FeS2 needs 11 O2 for 2 Fe2O3 and 8 SO2 (22 O atoms on each side).

1b.html:
A solid oxide film forms around the unreacted sulphide core (\mathrm{MS} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{SO_2}). \mathrm{O_2} must diffuse in and \mathrm{SO_2} out through it.

  1. The film grows thicker and its permeability to gases falls, so oxidation slows down.
  2. At the core \mathrm{O_2} falls and \mathrm{SO_2} rises, so the reaction tends to reverse.
  3. Some sulphur is held as sulphate at low temperature; heating harder risks sintering, which closes the pores.

So the last sulphur goes only slowly.
pts: An oxide film forms around the unreacted sulphide core as the particle is oxidised (\mathrm{MS} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{SO_2})
\mathrm{O_2} must diffuse in and \mathrm{SO_2} out through this layer; as it thickens its permeability falls and oxidation slows
Low \mathrm{O_2} and high \mathrm{SO_2} at the reaction front make the reaction slow down and tend to reverse
A further reason: sulphur held as sulphate at low temperature, or sintering at high temperature closes the pores
1b.watch:
• The key word is diffusion through the product layer; "the reaction is slow" without saying why earns little.
  • Remedies, if asked: fine grinding, rabbling or fluidising to expose fresh surface, excess air, and a longer time at temperature.
  • Draw the particle: sulphide core, oxide shell, O2 arrows in and SO2 arrows out. It takes one minute and carries the explanation.

1c.html:
Methods of roasting

The industrial roasting methods differ in how the sulphide particles are brought into contact with air.

  1. Multiple-hearth roasting. About 10 circular brick hearths are stacked inside a brick-lined steel shell. A rotating central shaft carries rabble arms whose rabbles plough the ore across each hearth to a drop hole, so the charge passes from hearth to hearth from top to bottom while air rises counter-current. Only surface particles meet air on a hearth; most roasting occurs while the ore falls between hearths. Slow, but easy to control, and the temperature is kept below sintering.
  2. Flash (suspension) roasting. Preheated, finely ground concentrate falls through a body of hot air in a combustion chamber, and the sulphur burns almost instantly ("flashing"). Very fast; needs fine grinding, and dust losses are high.
  3. Fluidised-bed roasting. The particles are roasted while suspended in an upward stream of air blown through a grid; the bed behaves like a boiling liquid. Gas-solid contact and mixing are excellent, the temperature is uniform (water spray control), capacity is high, and the calcine overflows continuously.
  4. Sinter (blast) roasting. On a Dwight-Lloyd machine, air is sucked down through a moving bed of fine concentrate ignited at the top; roasting and agglomeration happen together, giving a porous sinter for the blast furnace.

By chemistry, roasting is also classed as oxidising, sulphating, volatilising, chloridising or reducing.

Five stages of fluidisation (see the fluidisation curve)

  1. Fixed bed: at a very low gas flow the gas permeates the porous bed without disturbing the particles; the pressure drop is proportional to the flow rate (up to A).
  2. Expanded bed (AB): as the velocity rises the bed loosens and expands upward; the pressure drop still rises with velocity.
  3. Lifting point (BC): the pressure drop reaches the weight of the bed per unit area, with a small peak, at the minimum fluidisation velocity; the particles are just lifted.
  4. Fluidised (boiling) bed, beyond C: the pressure drop stays constant, independent of velocity; extra gas passes as bubbles and the bed flows like a liquid. The roaster works here.
  5. Entrainment (pneumatic transport): above the particles' terminal velocity they are carried out with the gas and the pressure drop falls; the roaster gas velocity is kept below this, and cyclones catch the carried-over fines.
pts: Multiple-hearth roaster: stacked hearths (about 10), rotating central shaft with rabble arms, ore drops hearth to hearth while air rises; most roasting during the fall
Flash (suspension) roaster: preheated fine concentrate falls through hot air and burns almost instantly; fine grinding needed, high dust loss
Fluidised-bed roaster: particles suspended in an upward air stream through a grid, liquid-like bed, good contact, uniform temperature, high capacity

Sinter roasting: Dwight-Lloyd machine, air drawn down through an ignited moving bed, roasting and agglomeration together (or the chemical types: oxidising, sulphating, volatilising, chloridising, reducing)
A comparison point: hearth roasting slow and controllable, flash and fluidised fast; or the temperature is kept below fusion in all of them
Stage 1, fixed bed: gas permeates without moving the particles; pressure drop proportional to flow rate
Stage 2, expanded bed: the bed expands upward and the pressure drop still rises with velocity (segment AB)
Stage 3, lifting point: pressure drop reaches the bed weight per unit area at the minimum fluidisation velocity (segment BC)
Stage 4, fluidised bed: pressure drop constant and independent of velocity, the bed flows like a liquid (point C onward); this is where roasting is done
Stage 5, entrainment or pneumatic transport above the terminal velocity, particles carried out, pressure drop falls
1c.watch:
• "Methods" here means the industrial roasters (the second sentence is about one of them); if you read it as the chemical types, still name the roasters in a line.
  • The slides describe four stages (fixed, expanded, lifting point, fluidised); the fifth, entrainment, is the textbook end of the curve. Some texts split stage 4 into smooth and bubbling (boiling) beds instead; either set of five earns the marks if each is described.
  • The slide says that at C "the expansion of the bed becomes independent of the gas velocity". The quantity that becomes independent is the pressure drop (it equals the bed weight per unit area); the bed itself still swells a little as bubbles pass.

2a.fix: • Page 2 of the reading (421-hydrobk) writes the gold ore grade as "10 ppm (10g l-1)". For a solid ore 10 ppm means 10 g of gold per tonne (10 mg per kg), not 10 g per litre.
2a.html:
Hydrometallurgy is the production of metals or pure metal compounds by reactions in aqueous (and sometimes organic) solutions, usually at room temperature or a little above it. It is a process of beneficiation as well as extraction: normally the value minerals are dissolved (leached) and the metal is recovered from the solution, but sometimes the gangue is leached first, as in the alkali leaching of monazite.

When it is preferred to pyrometallurgy

  1. Lean (low-grade) ores. Smelting would heat and slag all the gangue, but siliceous gangue is hardly attacked by most leaching reagents, so the reagent cost follows the metal content, not the tonnage. Gold ore with about 10 g/t (10 ppm) is leached with cyanide at a profit; smelting it is out of the question.
  2. Complex ores. The reactions are selective and every step can be controlled, so valuable by-products are recovered.
  3. Sulphide ores where SO2 is a problem. Leaching keeps the sulphur in solution (as sulphate or elemental S) instead of releasing SO2.
  4. Costly coke. Coke is the fuel and the reductant of most smelting, so a rising coke price favours the aqueous route.
  5. Small or growing output. A leach plant can start small and expand; a smelter is economic only on a large scale.
  6. Pure compounds or reactive metals, which are hard to refine by fire, for example pure \mathrm{Al_2O_3} from bauxite before reduction.

For rich ores and concentrates pyrometallurgy usually needs less energy per tonne of metal (concentrated streams, fast and often exothermic reactions).

Essential steps

  1. Leaching: selective dissolution of the desired elements in a leaching reagent, after any preparation (grinding, sizing, concentration, roasting), for example \mathrm{ZnO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2O}.
  2. Separation of the leach liquor from the solid residue by settling, thickening, filtration and washing.
  3. Recovery of the metal values from the liquor by precipitation, cementation, electrolysis, solvent extraction, ion exchange, evaporation or distillation.
  4. Recovery of the reagent: the spent solution is purified, its composition readjusted, and it is recycled to leaching (for example, \mathrm{H_2SO_4} is regenerated in copper electrowinning).
pts: Defines hydrometallurgy as producing metals or pure compounds by reactions in aqueous (or organic) solutions at low temperature, a beneficiation as well as an extraction process
Preferred for low-grade ores because the gangue is not heated or slagged and is largely unattacked, for example gold at about 10 g/t by cyanide
Preferred for complex ores, since selective, controlled steps recover by-products
Preferred for sulphide ores, since leaching avoids SO2 emission
Preferred where coke is costly, or where a small plant that can expand later is wanted
Preferred for pure compounds or reactive metals, or notes that for rich ores pyrometallurgy usually needs less energy
Step 1: leaching (selective dissolution in a reagent, after any grinding or roasting), with an example
Step 2: separation of the leach liquor from the residue (thickening, filtration, washing)
Step 3: recovery of the metal from the liquor, naming at least three methods (precipitation, cementation, electrolysis, solvent extraction, ion exchange)
Step 4: regeneration and recycling of the leaching reagent
2a.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 2-8; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 1-4
2a.watch:
• "Under what conditions" asks for situations, not a bare list of advantages; tie each advantage to the kind of ore or plant it suits.
  • The slides give four steps; the preparation of the ore (grinding, roasting) belongs to the leaching step, not a separate essential step.
  • Do not say hydrometallurgy always saves energy: for high-grade ores and concentrates the book says pyrometallurgy usually needs less energy per tonne of metal.

2b.html:
The leaching reagent R reacts at the mineral surface to give a soluble metal species M and other products P. Two situations can arise (see the sketches).

(a) The mineral dissolves completely. All the products are soluble, so the surface simply recedes and no solid layer forms, for example \mathrm{ZnO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2O}. Across the liquid boundary film the reagent falls from [R]_B in the bulk to [R]_S at the surface, while M and P are highest at the surface and fall to [M]_B and [P]_B. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk of the solution to the mineral-solution interface;
  2. reaction of R with the mineral surface to form the soluble metal species;
  3. diffusion of M (and P) away from the interface into the bulk.

(b) The mineral decomposes and dissolves in parts. An insoluble product, or the undissolved part of the ore, stays behind as a porous residue around the unreacted mineral; leaching goes on only if this layer is porous. Example: \mathrm{CaWO_4(s) + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow CaCO_3(s) + WO_4^{2-}}. I is the mineral-residue interface and II the residue-solution interface. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk to the residue-solution interface II;
  2. diffusion of R through the porous residue to I;
  3. reaction of R with the mineral at I to form soluble M;
  4. outward diffusion of M and P through the porous layer;
  5. diffusion of M and P from II into the bulk.

Case (a) lacks steps 2 and 4. The slowest step, or a combination, controls the rate.

Accelerating the leaching. Find the rate-controlling step first, then:

  • Film diffusion (steps 1 or 5): stir the solution. The boundary layer thins and the gradients steepen, so the rate rises with stirring speed until it levels off.
  • Chemical reaction (step 3): agitation has no effect. Raise the temperature (activation energy about 10 to 25 kcal/mol, so the rate is very sensitive to it), the reagent concentration (by the reaction order) or the oxidant supply.
  • Pore diffusion (steps 2 and 4): grind finer, which shortens the path and raises the surface area (10 mm to 0.1 mm gives 100 times the area per unit mass), or roast first to make the solid porous.
  • A higher temperature speeds up all the steps, diffusion only weakly (5 kcal/mol or less).
pts: Sketch (a): mineral, solution and boundary film, with [R] rising from [R]_S to [R]_B and [M], [P] falling from the surface to the bulk
Sketch (b): mineral, porous residue with interfaces I and II, and the [R], [M], [P] profiles across residue and film
Explains situation (a): complete dissolution with soluble products and no solid layer, with an example
Explains situation (b): partial decomposition leaving a porous residue (leaching goes on only if it is porous), with an example
Three steps for (a): diffusion of R in, surface reaction, diffusion of M and P out
Five steps for (b): film diffusion of R, pore diffusion of R, reaction at I, pore diffusion of M and P, film diffusion of M and P
Stirring speeds up leaching when film diffusion (step 1 or 5) controls, but has no effect when the chemical reaction (step 3) controls
Raising the temperature speeds up all steps, the chemical reaction most (higher activation energy)
A further method tied to its step: finer grinding (surface area, shorter pore path), higher reagent or oxidant concentration, or roasting to make the solid porous
2b.sketch:
• (a): hatched mineral, solution, liquid boundary film; [R] rising from [R]_S at the surface to [R]_B; [M] and [P] falling from [M]_S, [P]_S to the bulk.
  • (b): mineral, porous residue between interfaces I and II, solution; [R] rising from [R]_I through [R]_{II} to the bulk; [M] and [P] falling from I to II to the bulk.
  • Arrows for R moving in and for M and P moving out, numbered as the kinetic steps.
2b.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 13-17; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 4-5, 13-15
2b.watch:
• The slides number the steps of case (b) 1 to 5 and say "step 1 or step 5" for film diffusion and "step 3" for the reaction; in case (a) these are its steps 1, 3 and 2. Keep your numbering consistent with your sketch.
  • Even when more stirring stops helping, diffusion across the limiting film may still control; the activation energy (diffusion 5 kcal/mol or less, reaction 10 to 25 kcal/mol, that is 21 and 42 to 105 kJ/mol) tells which.
  • Extra depth: for a shrinking particle of radius R_0, the time for complete leaching grows as R_0 under reaction control and as R_0^2 under diffusion through a residue layer, so grinding helps most when pore diffusion controls.

3a.html:
A Pachuca vat is an air-agitated tank used in agitation (slime) leaching: finely ground ore or concentrate (about 200 µm) is kept in suspension in the leaching solution as a pulp.

Construction. A tall cylindrical tank, typically about 4 m in diameter and 15 m high, with a conical bottom, made of wood or rubber-lined steel. A central vertical pipe, coaxial with the tank and open at both ends, runs from just above the cone to just below the pulp surface. Compressed air is blown in at the lower end of this pipe.

How leaching is accomplished (air lift).

  1. The air bubbles in the central pipe make the pulp inside it lighter than the pulp around it.
  2. The heavier surrounding pulp pushes the aerated pulp up the pipe; it overflows at the top.
  3. The pulp then flows down the annulus between pipe and wall, and the cone guides it back into the foot of the pipe, so the whole charge circulates and the solids cannot settle.
  4. The constant renewal of liquid at the particle surfaces speeds up the diffusion of reagent in and of dissolved metal out.
  5. The air also aerates the pulp, supplying the oxygen that some leaching reactions consume, for example gold cyanidation:
\mathrm{4Au + 8NaCN + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4NaAu(CN)_2 + 4NaOH}
  1. Live steam can be injected with the air to heat the pulp to about 60 to 70 degrees C.

Pulp is fed at the top and discharged after the required time, batchwise or through several vats in series, and then goes to thickening and filtration to separate the pregnant solution. The vat is very simple and has no moving parts, so it seldom breaks down; it is widely used for slime leaching, notably of gold ores.
pts: Sketch: tall cylindrical tank with a conical bottom and a central tube open at both ends
Sketch: compressed-air inlet at the bottom of the central tube, with pulp inlet and outlet
Sketch: circulation arrows, up the central tube and down the annulus
States its use: agitation (slime) leaching of finely ground ore kept in suspension as a pulp
Construction details: about 4 m in diameter and 15 m high, wood or rubber-lined steel
Explains the air lift: bubbles lower the pulp density in the tube, the denser outer pulp forces it up, it overflows and returns down the annulus, circulating the whole charge
Aeration supplies the oxygen consumed in leaching, with an example such as gold cyanidation
Heating by live steam injected with the air (up to about 60 to 70 degrees C)
No moving parts, so simple and low in maintenance

  • Central tube, open at both ends, with the compressed-air pipe entering its lower end.
  • Arrows: pulp rising in the tube with the bubbles, overflowing at the top, falling in the annulus and re-entering at the cone.
  • Pulp inlet and outlet.

3b.fix: • Slide 65 (and the course book p 28) writes the elution step as \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl \rightarrow 4RCl + UO_2(SO_4)}. Sulphur (3 against 1) and charge do not balance, and chloride must be \mathrm{Cl^-}. The uranium returns to solution as \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, or equivalently \mathrm{UO_2SO_4 + 2SO_4^{2-}}, as written in the Answer. The book's loading equation also prints \mathrm{2SO_3^{-4}} for \mathrm{2SO_4^{2-}}.
3b.html:
Why the leach liquor is purified

Leaching is rarely completely selective, so the pregnant liquor also carries ions that interfere with later steps or would leave unacceptable impurity levels in the product. Purification lowers their concentration, or removes the desired metal selectively and leaves the impurities behind. The common methods are selective precipitation, ion exchange and solvent extraction.

Principle

Metal ions in solution exchange with specific ions held by a solid (a resin) or by a second liquid phase. The exchange is reversible and stoichiometric, so it can (i) remove unwanted ions from the solution and (ii) concentrate a selected metal ion.

The resin is an insoluble, chemically stable, rigid 3-D polymer framework, made as small hard porous beads (0.5-1 mm) of high surface area. Functional groups bonded to the framework supply the exchangeable ions: the framework fixes the physical properties, the functional groups control the selectivity.

\begin{aligned} \text{cation exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{2\,R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}\\ \text{anion exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{R^+Cl^- + A^- \rightleftharpoons R^+A^- + Cl^-} \end{aligned}

The cycle

  1. Loading (sorption): clear pregnant liquor flows through columns of resin; the resin takes up the metal ion and releases its own ion. The barren solution is dumped.
  2. Elution (stripping): a relatively small volume of strong solution reverses the reaction, giving a concentrated, pure eluate.
  3. Regeneration: the resin is returned to its original form, ready for sorption again.

Example: uranium from sulphuric acid leach liquor

Uranium forms the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, while the impurity metals are mostly cations, so an anion-exchange resin takes up the uranium and leaves the impurities in solution. Low-grade ores (about 0.2 % \mathrm{U_3O_8}) are treated this way.

\begin{aligned} \text{loading:}&\quad \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-} + 2R_2SO_4 \rightarrow R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 2SO_4^{2-}}\\ \text{elution (acidified chloride):}&\quad \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl^- \rightarrow 4RCl + [UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}\\ \text{regeneration:}&\quad \mathrm{4RCl + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2R_2SO_4 + 4HCl} \end{aligned}

Plant practice (resin-in-column)

Columns A and B load in series while C is eluted. When A is saturated it goes to elution, B leads and the freshly eluted C becomes the tail; the change-overs repeat endlessly. The flow is counter-current: fresh liquor meets nearly loaded resin, and fresh resin meets nearly exhausted liquor.

Why it purifies and concentrates

Ions the resin does not take stay in the barren solution (purification). Loading and elution are almost 100 % efficient, so the concentration factor is about V_{\text{liquor}}/V_{\text{eluate}} (concentration). The exchange depends on the size and valence of the ions, their concentration, the nature of the resin and the temperature.
pts: Need for purification: leaching is not selective, impurities interfere or contaminate the product; ion exchange is one of the methods (with selective precipitation and solvent extraction)
Principle: ions in solution exchange with ions held on a solid resin (or a second liquid); reversible and stoichiometric; removes unwanted ions or concentrates a selected one
Resin: insoluble, chemically stable 3-D polymer framework as porous beads (about 0.5-1 mm); bonded functional groups supply the exchangeable ions and control selectivity
A general exchange reaction for a cation or an anion exchanger, for example \mathrm{2R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}
The cycle: loading in columns, elution with a small volume of strong solution to give a concentrated eluate, regeneration of the resin
Uranium is the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}} while impurities are cations, so an anion resin is selective
Uranium reactions for loading, elution with chloride and regeneration (1 each; elution balanced with the uranyl sulphate complex, or \mathrm{UO_2SO_4 + 2SO_4^{2-}})
Plant: resin in tall columns, A and B loading in series while C is eluted, then change-over; counter-current contact
Purification (impurity ions stay in the barren solution) and concentration (eluate volume much smaller, nearly 100 % efficient steps)
Factors: ion size and valence, concentration, nature of the resin, temperature

3b.watch:
• No sketch is asked, so none is credited; the column figure only shows the change-over.
  • In the uranium equations \mathrm{R^+} is the fixed quaternary ammonium group of the anion resin, so \mathrm{R_2SO_4} is the resin in its sulphate form and RCl in its chloride form.

4a.html:
Mechanism of electrolysis

Electrolysis is the decomposition of an electrolyte by direct current, which drives a non-spontaneous reaction (\Delta G > 0).

  1. Ions carry the current in the electrolyte (fused salt or solution), e.g. \mathrm{CuSO_4 \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + SO_4^{2-}}; electrons carry it in the electrodes and external circuit.
  2. Migration: the DC source feeds electrons to the cathode (-) and withdraws them from the anode (+); cations move to the cathode, anions to the anode, aided by diffusion and convection.
  3. Charge transfer: at the cathode, reduction, \mathrm{M^{z+} + z\,e^- \rightarrow M} (or \mathrm{H_2} evolution). At the anode, oxidation: a soluble anode dissolves, \mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{z+} + z\,e^-}; an insoluble one evolves gas, \mathrm{H_2O \rightarrow \tfrac12 O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^-}.
  4. Driving force: the applied voltage must exceed the decomposition voltage; the mass deposited follows Faraday's law, m = ItM/(zF).

Example, copper electrowinning on a lead anode (acid regenerated for leaching):

\mathrm{CuSO_4 + H_2O \rightarrow Cu + \tfrac12 O_2 + H_2SO_4}

Essential requirements for an electrochemical reaction

  1. Two electrodes (electronic conductors): an anode for oxidation and a cathode for reduction.
  2. An electrolyte: an ionic conductor touching both electrodes and containing the reacting ions.
  3. A closed external circuit, so the electrons released at the anode reach the cathode.
  4. A driving force: negative \Delta G = -zFE (galvanic cell), or an applied voltage of at least the decomposition voltage plus the IR drop (electrolytic cell).
pts: States that the electrolyte (aqueous or fused) contains ions that carry the current, while electrons carry it in the electrodes and the external circuit
Cations migrate to the cathode and anions to the anode under the applied DC field (with diffusion and convection)
Cathode reduction \mathrm{M^{z+} + ze^- \rightarrow M} and anode oxidation (soluble anode dissolves, or a gas such as \mathrm{O_2} evolves on an insoluble anode), with an example
Electrolysis is non-spontaneous: it needs a voltage above the decomposition voltage, and the mass follows Faraday's law
Requirement: an anode and a cathode (electronic conductors)
Requirement: an electrolyte (ionic conductor) in contact with both
Requirement: a closed external circuit so electrons flow from the anode to the cathode
Requirement: a driving force, negative \Delta G (galvanic) or an applied voltage at least the decomposition voltage (electrolytic)
4a.src: Standard textbook treatment; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), p 6
4a.watch:
• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • Do not swap the signs: in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive, in a galvanic cell it is negative, but oxidation is always at the anode.
  • Write both electrode reactions with balanced charge; a mechanism without electrode reactions earns little.

4b.html:
At the cathode the reduction with the most positive deposition potential goes first. In an aqueous electrolyte the metal ion always competes with hydrogen:

\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}} = -0.0592\,\mathrm{pH} - \eta_{\mathrm{H}}\ \ (25^\circ\mathrm{C})
\mathrm{M^{z+} + z\,e^- \rightarrow M}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{M}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}} + \frac{0.0592}{z}\log a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}} - \eta_{\mathrm{M}}

where \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is the hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode surface. The metal deposits when E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}}.

Metals less reactive (nobler) than hydrogen

  • Cu (+0.34 V), Ag (+0.80 V), Au (+1.50 V) have E^\circ > 0. Even at a low ion activity (10^{-3} gives +0.25 V for Cu) the metal potential stays above that of hydrogen, so the metal deposits in preference to hydrogen, even from strongly acid solution.
  • Copper is electrowon from \mathrm{CuSO_4} with about 150-180 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 85-95 % current efficiency.
  • Hydrogen appears mainly when the current density approaches the limiting current of metal-ion diffusion; the deposit then becomes powdery and spongy. So the current density is kept below it.

Metals more reactive than hydrogen

  • Zn (-0.76 V), Fe (-0.44 V), Ni (-0.25 V) have E^\circ < 0. By equilibrium, hydrogen should be discharged first and no metal should deposit.
  • They deposit because hydrogen discharge is slow on many metals: the hydrogen overvoltage (about 0.7-1 V on Zn, Pb, Sn, Hg; below 0.1 V on Pt) pushes E_{\mathrm{H}} below E_{\mathrm{M}}.
  • Deposition is favoured by a cathode metal with high \eta_{\mathrm{H}}, high current density, low temperature, high metal-ion concentration, a higher pH (below hydroxide precipitation) and an electrolyte purified of Co, Ni, Sb, Ge, which lower \eta_{\mathrm{H}}.
  • Zinc: from about 150-200 g/L acid at 35-40 ^\circC and 400-600 A/m^2 on Al cathodes, current efficiency about 90 %.
  • Fe, Ni, Co have low hydrogen overvoltage, so they need a weakly acid (pH about 2-4), warm electrolyte and give lower efficiency.
  • Very reactive metals (Al -1.66 V, Mg -2.37 V, Na -2.71 V): no attainable overvoltage stops hydrogen evolution, and any deposit reacts with water, e.g. \mathrm{2Al + 6H_2O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_2}. They are won by fused-salt electrolysis (Hall-Heroult for Al).
pts: Nobler metals (Cu, Ag, Au; E^\circ > 0) deposit in preference to hydrogen, even from acid solution, because their potential is more positive
Uses the Nernst equation (or the cathode rule "most positive potential first") to show the metal still deposits at low ion activity or high acidity
Hydrogen evolves mainly near the limiting current density, spoiling the deposit; current efficiency is high (Cu about 85-95 %)
Metals more reactive than hydrogen (E^\circ < 0): thermodynamically hydrogen should be discharged first
Hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode (high on Zn, Pb, Hg, low on Pt) lowers the hydrogen potential below that of the metal, so the metal deposits
Conditions that favour deposition: high current density, low temperature, high metal concentration, pH control, purified electrolyte (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge removed); zinc as the example
Fe, Ni, Co (low overvoltage) need a weakly acid electrolyte (pH about 2-4) and give lower efficiency
Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na) cannot be deposited from water and are won by fused-salt electrolysis
4b.watch:
• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • "Less reactive than hydrogen" means a more positive standard potential (nobler), not a lower one; keep the sign convention of reduction potentials.
  • Overvoltage values depend on current density, temperature and surface state; quote them as "about", and give the trend (Hg, Pb, Zn high; Pt low).
  • Mercury cathodes allow even Na to be discharged as an amalgam (chlor-alkali cells), because the overvoltage on Hg is high and Na activity in the amalgam is low; this is the exception to the last point.

4c.html:
An impurity behaves according to its electrode potential relative to the metal being treated.

In electrorefining (impurities in the anode)

  1. Nobler than the metal (Au, Ag, Pt metals in Cu): they do not dissolve and fall as anode slime, a valuable by-product.
  2. Less noble (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co in Cu): they dissolve with the anode and accumulate in the electrolyte, but do not deposit (far more negative potentials); a bleed keeps them low.
  3. Close to the metal in potential (As, Sb, Bi in Cu): they partly dissolve and may co-deposit, or form "floating slime" that is trapped in the cathode. Most troublesome; controlled by bleeding and liberator cells.
  4. Insoluble compounds: \mathrm{Cu_2Se}, \mathrm{Cu_2Te} and \mathrm{Ag_2Se} go to the slime; Pb dissolves and re-precipitates as \mathrm{PbSO_4}; Sn forms an insoluble basic salt or oxide.

In electrowinning (impurities in the electrolyte)

  1. Ions nobler than the metal won (Cu, Cd, Co in zinc electrolyte) co-deposit and contaminate the cathode, so the solution is purified first (zinc-dust cementation).
  2. Impurities that lower the hydrogen overvoltage (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge in zinc winning) cause hydrogen evolution and re-dissolve the deposit. Ions with two valencies (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}) shuttle between the electrodes. Both lower the current efficiency.
pts: Nobler impurities (Au, Ag, Pt metals) do not dissolve and report to the anode slime
Less noble impurities (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co) dissolve and accumulate in the electrolyte without depositing; removed by bleeding the electrolyte
Impurities close in potential (As, Sb, Bi) partly dissolve and can co-deposit or form floating slime; controlled by bleeding or liberator cells
Insoluble compounds and precipitates (selenides, tellurides, \mathrm{PbSO_4}, tin compounds) go to the slime
In electrowinning, ions nobler than the metal co-deposit, so the solution is purified before electrolysis (e.g. zinc-dust cementation)
Impurities that lower hydrogen overvoltage (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge in Zn) or that change valency (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}) lower the current efficiency
4c.watch:
• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • Build the answer on the potential order (noble, base, close to the metal); a bare list of impurities earns little.
  • Ag is partly soluble in the copper electrolyte; a little chloride is added so that it precipitates as AgCl and reports to the slime.

5a.html:
Definition. Ore dressing (mineral processing, beneficiation) is the treatment of ore, mainly by physical methods and sometimes by limited chemical ones, that separates the value minerals from the gangue. It gives a concentrate rich in the value mineral and tailings lean in it, so the concentrate can be treated economically for metal extraction; no metal is produced. The ore is crushed and ground to liberate the value mineral, then separated by differences in specific gravity, magnetism, electrical conductivity or surface wettability (flotation).

Benefits.

  1. Saving in freight: the gangue is discarded at the mine, so far less tonnage is shipped.
  2. Lower total extraction cost: less tonnage to heat, flux or leach, so less fuel, flux and energy. Upgrading 1% Cu ore to a 25% Cu concentrate cuts the smelter feed about 25-fold.
  3. Smaller metal losses: less gangue means less slag, so less metal is lost in it.
  4. Expansion of ore reserves: rock below 1% Cu was not processed in the last century; today 0.5% Cu rock is.
  5. Cleaner feed: fewer impurities reach the crude metal, and complex Cu-Pb-Zn ores give separate concentrates.

These gains must outweigh the dressing cost and the metal lost to tailings.
pts: Defines ore dressing as the (mainly physical) separation of value minerals from gangue that gives a concentrate and tailings before extraction
Notes that comminution liberates the mineral and that separation uses physical or surface properties (specific gravity, magnetism, conductivity, wettability); no metal is produced
Benefit: saving in freight because the gangue is discarded at the mine
Benefit: lower total extraction cost because of the reduced tonnage (less fuel, flux, reagent and energy)
Benefit: smaller metal losses because less slag is made
Benefit: expansion of ore reserves, with the example that Cu rock below 1% was not processed but 0.5% Cu rock is processed today
A further benefit (purer crude metal or separate concentrates from complex ores) and the caveat that dressing cost and tailings losses must be weighed
5a.src: Introduction (sources, recycling, overview), slides 29-30, 34; Book Ch 1 reading, pp 25-27
5a.watch:
• "Define" needs one clear sentence with the words value mineral, gangue, concentrate and tailings; a list of methods is not a definition.
  • The book lists three benefits (freight, extraction cost, metal losses) and adds the expansion of reserves; give all four.
  • Ore dressing can include chemical steps such as a magnetising roast, which turns weakly magnetic iron oxide into magnetite (\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}) for magnetic separation. The concentrate is still a mineral, not metal.

5b.html:
A mineral is a specific natural compound: galena (PbS) is always galena. A deposit is an ore only if a metal can be extracted from it at a profit, so a galena-bearing rock may be lead ore at one time and mere rock at another. The boundary moves with:

  1. Metal price: a higher price, other things equal, makes a lower-grade deposit economic; a price fall turns marginal ore back into rock.
  2. Technology: around 1900, rock with less than 1% Pb was not an ore; since froth flotation, lead is extracted at a profit from 0.3% Pb ore. Likewise for Cu: 1% once, 0.5% today.
  3. New uses: magnesite used only for refractories was a non-metallic mineral; now that it is a source of magnesium, it is an ore of Mg.
  4. Cost, access and law: deep-sea manganese nodules at about 5000 m remain only a resource until their collection is economic and permitted.

So "mineral" is a fixed scientific term, while "ore" is an economic one.
pts: States the test: a mineral is a fixed compound (galena is always galena), but a deposit is an ore only if the metal can be extracted at a profit, so the boundary moves
Price: a higher metal price makes a lower-grade deposit an ore, and a price fall reverses it
Technology example with numbers: the lead ore limit fell from 1% to 0.3% Pb after froth flotation, or Cu from 1% to 0.5%
New-use example: magnesite changed from a refractory (non-metallic) mineral to an ore of Mg
A cost, access or legal factor, for example manganese nodules at about 5000 m that are not yet mined
Concludes that "mineral" is a scientific term and "ore" an economic one
5b.src: Introduction (sources, recycling, overview), slides 23, 34; Book Ch 1 reading, pp 3, 20, 26-27
5b.watch:
• The examples carry the marks in "explain with examples": quote the 1% to 0.3% Pb figure and name froth flotation as the technology.
  • Keep the definitions short; this part asks why the boundary moves, not for a full comparison of ores and minerals.
  • Coal is not called an ore at any price, because no metal is extracted from it.

5c.html:
Recycling as a source of metals

Metals from ores are primary metals; metals from scrap are secondary metals. Recycling has become a major source because:

  1. Scrap is already metallic. It needs only refining, at best only melting. Primary metal needs mining, ore dressing and the reduction of the oxide or sulphide (breaking metal-oxygen or metal-sulphur bonds); recycling skips all of these.
  2. Energy and CO2 savings. Energy saved is about 95% for Al, 85% for Cu and 60-75% for steel; CO2 falls by about 90%, 65% and 50%. Primary metallurgy gives about 7-9% of world CO2.
  3. Fewer, simpler operations: no mining, dressing, roasting or smelting, so less pollution, land and water use, and no tailings.
  4. Conservation of resources. High-grade deposits are limited: copper ores fell from about 4% Cu a century ago to 1% or less, so primary metal costs ever more energy.
  5. Demand and security. Metal demand may double by 2050 (EVs, wind, solar); urban mining supplies Cu, Au and critical metals (Li, Co, rare earths).
  6. Equal quality. No test distinguishes secondary from primary metal; some of the best stainless steels are made wholly from scrap. In Bangladesh about 75% of steelmaking scrap (about 1.5 Mt in 2005) came from ship-breaking.

Classification of scrap by availability

  1. Home scrap: generated in the plant during primary or secondary metal production, such as defective castings and sheet edge trimmings. Known composition, no collection or sorting; always recycled at once.
  2. Prompt industrial scrap: generated while manufacturing metal articles, such as turnings and stamping offcuts; machining can yield up to 50% scrap. Clean and returned quickly; its amount follows manufacturing activity.
  3. Obsolete scrap: products at the end of their life, such as old rails, machinery, cars and ships. Supply depends on product lifetime (car 10-12 years, lead-acid battery 2-4 years) and scrap price; it is mixed and must be collected and sorted. It offers the largest scope for more recycling.
pts: Scrap is already in the metallic state, so only melting and refining are needed and the bond-breaking (reduction) energy is saved
Quotes energy savings: about 95% for Al, 85% for Cu, 60-75% for steel
Fewer, simpler operations give less pollution and CO2 (CO2 cuts about 90% Al, 65% Cu, 50% steel, or primary metal is about 7-9% of world CO2), no mine or tailings
Conservation of limited high-grade ore: Cu grade fell from about 4% to 1% or less, so primary metal costs more energy over time
Rising demand, urban mining or critical metals, or the point that secondary metal equals primary in quality (stainless from scrap, ship scrap in Bangladesh)
Home scrap: defined as scrap from metal production, with an example (defective castings, trimmings), always recycled in the plant
Prompt industrial scrap: defined as scrap from manufacturing, with an example (turnings, offcuts, up to 50% from machining), returned quickly
Obsolete scrap: defined as end-of-life products, with examples (cars, rails, ships), depends on lifetime and price and needs collection and sorting
5c.sketch:
• A loop diagram: ore, then primary metal production, then manufacturing, then products in use, then end of life.
  • An arrow from metal production back to the furnace labelled "home scrap".
  • An arrow from manufacturing back to the furnace labelled "prompt industrial scrap".
  • An arrow from end of life through "collection and sorting" to "secondary metal production", labelled "obsolete scrap".

5c.watch:
• "Justify" needs reasons with numbers; one line on "saves energy" earns little. The energy table is the strongest evidence.
  • Do not swap home and prompt scrap: home scrap comes from the metal producer, prompt scrap from the manufacturer that uses the metal.
  • Home and prompt scrap are recycled whatever the scrap price; obsolete scrap is price-sensitive, which is why most of the room for growth lies there.
  • Extra depth: an automobile graveyard is called an iron mine above ground; in 2003 the US recycled nearly 13 million vehicles, giving more than 14 Mt of shredded steel scrap.

6a.html:
Size reduction is done in stages, with a different machine for each stage:

  1. Primary (coarse) crushers take run-of-mine ore (feed up to about 1500 mm): jaw crushers (Blake, Dodge) and gyratory crushers.
  2. Secondary (intermediate) crushers take the primary product: cone crushers (a faster relative of the gyratory), roll crushers (smooth and toothed) and stamp mills.
  3. Grinding (tumbling or revolving) mills take crushed ore and grind it below about 6 mm: rod mills, ball mills and autogenous mills.

In the general chemical-engineering grouping the principal types are crushers, grinders, ultrafine grinders and cutting machines.
pts: Primary crushers: jaw (Blake or Dodge) and gyratory
Secondary crushers: cone and roll crushers (smooth and toothed), or stamp mills
Tumbling mills for grinding: rod, ball and autogenous mills
Notes that the machines are used in stages by size (crushing to about 6 mm, grinding below it), or names ultrafine grinders and cutting machines
6a.src: Size reduction, slides 3-6, 8, 15, 18-19, 23, 32; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 1, 3, 7-10
6a.watch:
• "List" wants names grouped by stage, not descriptions; one line each is enough for 5 marks.
  • The slides split the stages into crushing, grinding (1 to 5 mm) and milling (rod and ball mills); the book reading calls everything below about 6 mm grinding. Either grouping earns the marks if the machines are right. Slide 5 puts the cone crusher under grinding, but it is a secondary crusher (slide 18).
  • Impact machines such as hammer mills are not in the course slides but are a correct extra.

6b.html:
In a Blake crusher the swing jaw hangs from a pivot at the top and is driven at the bottom by an eccentric, a pitman and two toggle plates. The jaw acts as a lever.

Step 1, model. Let the pivot be O, the toggle push P act normal to the jaw at the bottom, a distance L from O, and a lump touch the jaw a distance x from O and push back on it with force F. Friction and the weight of the jaw are neglected; the slow crushing stroke is quasi-static.

Step 2, moments about the pivot.

F\,x = P\,L \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{F = \frac{P\,L}{x}}

With several lumps, \sum F_i x_i = PL. The force on a lump varies as 1/x: largest near the pivot, least at the throat.

Step 3, toggle force. The pitman pulls the toggle joint up with force Q; each toggle makes a small angle \theta with the horizontal and carries thrust T. At the joint, 2T\sin\theta = Q, and the horizontal push on the jaw is

P = T\cos\theta = \frac{Q}{2\tan\theta} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{F = \frac{Q\,L}{2\,x\tan\theta}}

As the toggles straighten (\theta \to 0) the force multiplies greatly.

Step 4, movement. The jaw turns through a small angle \delta\phi, so the movement at x is s = x\,\delta\phi and at the throat s_L = L\,\delta\phi (the throw). Then F s = P s_L: the same work, but near the pivot as large force with small movement.

Step 5, where the large lumps sit. With gape G and jaw angle \beta (20 to 30 degrees), the opening at x is about G - x\tan\beta. A lump of size d lodges where the opening equals d:

x_d = \frac{G - d}{\tan\beta} \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_d = \frac{P\,L\tan\beta}{G - d}

F_d rises as d approaches G: the largest lumps lodge high, near the pivot, and receive the largest force.

Interpretation. A large lump needs a large force (about proportional to its cross-section, d^2) but little movement, since rock breaks at small strain. Small pieces at the throat need less force, and the large movement there gives free discharge, so a Blake crusher rarely chokes.

Example (illustrative): L = 1.2 m, \theta = 10^\circ, Q = 100 kN give P = 283.6 kN. A lump at x = 0.3 m receives F = 4P = 1134 kN; one at the throat 283.6 kN. With a 12 mm throw, the movement at 0.3 m is 3 mm, and Fs = Ps_L = 3.40 kJ at both points.
pts: Models the swing jaw as a lever pivoted at the top, with the toggle push P at distance L and a lump at distance x (friction and jaw weight neglected)
Takes moments about the pivot: Fx = PL
Concludes F = PL/x, so the force is greatest near the pivot and least at the throat
Toggle mechanics: 2T\sin\theta = Q, P = Q/(2\tan\theta), so F = QL/(2x\tan\theta) and the force multiplies as the toggles straighten
Movement s = x\,\delta\phi, largest at the throat, with the work relation Fs = Ps_L
Shows that a lump of size d lodges at x_d = (G-d)/\tan\beta, so the largest lumps sit nearest the pivot and receive the largest force
Explains why this suits crushing: large lumps need large force and little strain; large movement at the bottom gives free discharge and no choking
A consistent numerical illustration (for example F = 4P at x = L/4)

• Fixed jaw vertical; swing jaw hanging from a pivot O at the top, closing toward the fixed jaw at the bottom.
  • Toggle plates and pitman at the bottom, with the pitman pull Q, the toggle angle \theta and the thrust P at distance L.
  • A large lump near the top with a long force arrow F_1 and a small lump near the throat with a short arrow F_2; distance x marked from O.

6b.watch:
• Measure x from the pivot, not from the throat; with x from the bottom the 1/x result is lost.
  • In a Dodge crusher the pivot is at the bottom, so the large movement is at the top, the discharge opening hardly changes, and it tends to choke: the opposite of the Blake design.
  • The numbers in the example are illustrative; the printed question gives none, so any consistent example earns the mark.
  • The toggle result is the classic toggle-joint advantage: at \theta = 5^\circ the push is 5.7Q, at \theta = 10^\circ it is 2.8Q.

6c.html:
Critical speed is the speed of rotation at which a single particle (ball) is just held against the shell wall for a full revolution, because at the top of the shell the centrifugal force equals its weight.

Derivation. Take a ball of mass M, small compared with the mill of diameter D (m), riding on the shell at speed v. At the top of the shell both the weight and the wall's reaction N point toward the centre:

N + Mg = \frac{Mv^2}{D/2} = \frac{2Mv^2}{D}

The ball stays on the wall while N \geq 0. At the critical speed N = 0:

Mg = \frac{2Mv^2}{D} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v^2 = \frac{gD}{2}

With N in revolutions per minute, v = \pi D N/60:

\begin{aligned} \frac{\pi^2 D^2 N_c^2}{3600} &= \frac{gD}{2} \\ N_c &= \frac{60}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g}{2D}} = \frac{60}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{9.81}{2}}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}} \end{aligned}
\boxed{N_c = \frac{42.3}{\sqrt{D}}\ \mathrm{rpm}\quad (D\ \text{in m})}

For a ball of diameter d, its centre runs on a circle of diameter D - d, so N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{D - d}.

Example: a 2 m mill has N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{2} = 29.9 rpm; at the usual 65 to 82% of N_c it runs at 19.4 to 24.5 rpm.

Too high (at or above N_c): the charge is held against the shell all the way round (centrifuging). There is no relative motion between balls and ore, so hardly any grinding occurs, while power is still consumed.

Too low: the balls are not lifted high; they simply roll down the inner surface (cascading). There is little impact and only limited grinding, mostly by abrasion, so capacity is low.

Mills therefore run at about 65 to 82% of the critical speed with 30 to 50% of the volume filled, so that balls are lifted and fall onto the toe of the charge.
pts: Defines critical speed as the speed at which a ball is just held against the shell for a full revolution (centrifugal force equals weight at the top)
Force balance at the top: Mg = 2Mv^2/D (or M\omega^2 D/2), with the reason that the wall reaction becomes zero
Substitutes v = \pi DN/60 and rearranges correctly
Result N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{D} rpm with D in metres (or 42.3/\sqrt{D-d})
A worked number or the operating range of 65 to 82% of N_c
Too high: charge centrifuges and sticks to the shell, so hardly any grinding
Too low: balls roll down the surface (cascading), little impact, limited grinding by abrasion only
6c.src: Size reduction, slides 27, 29; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 14-15
6c.watch:
• Carry the units: D in metres gives N_c in rpm. With D in feet the constant becomes 76.6.
  • The force balance uses the radius D/2. Taking the radius as D in M\omega^2 r = Mg gives 29.9/\sqrt{D}, the wrong constant.
  • "Critical speed" is not the best speed: a mill at N_c does almost no grinding.

7a.html:
Classification is a method of separating mineral particles of various sizes, shapes and specific gravities into two or more products on the basis of the velocity with which they fall through a fluid (usually water). Coarse, heavier and rounder grains settle faster than finer, lighter and more angular ones. It is used for particles too fine to be screened efficiently.

Principle.

  1. A particle falling in a fluid is accelerated by gravity (less buoyancy), while the fluid resistance grows with its velocity.
  2. When gravity balances buoyancy plus resistance, the particle reaches its terminal velocity and then falls at a uniform rate.
  3. At low velocity the resistance is viscous (shear in the fluid); at high velocity it is turbulent (displacement of fluid). In the viscous range, Stokes' law gives
v_t = \frac{d^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)\,g}{18\,\mu}

so for equal density the larger particle falls faster, and for equal size the denser one does.

  1. In a sorting column the fluid rises at a uniform velocity V. Particles with v_t > V sink and leave as the spigot product; those with v_t < V are carried into the overflow.
  2. Free and hindered settling. Below about 15% solids particles settle freely and size dominates; in denser pulps the pulp acts as a heavy liquid and density gains weight.
pts: Defines classification as separation into two or more products by the velocity of fall through a fluid, which depends on size, specific gravity and shape
States that coarse, heavy, round grains settle faster and that it is used for particles too fine to screen
Gravity accelerates the particle while resistance rises with velocity; at balance the particle reaches terminal velocity and falls uniformly
Viscous resistance at low and turbulent at high velocity, with Stokes' law v_t = d^2(\rho_s-\rho_f)g/18\mu or the size and density rule
Sorting column (described or sketched): fluid rising at V; particles with v_t > V go to the spigot, v_t < V to the overflow
Free settling below about 15% solids (size dominant) against hindered settling in denser pulps (pulp acts as a heavy liquid, density gains weight)
7a.sketch:
• A vertical column with the fluid rising at velocity V (arrows up).
  • Overflow at the top labelled "v_t < V" (fine, light); spigot product at the bottom labelled "v_t > V" (coarse, dense).
  • Optional: a particle with weight down and buoyancy and drag up.
7a.src: Particle selection (supersedes the 72-slide version), slides 18, 28-30; Particle selection reading 1 (book Ch 3), pp 18, 21; Standard textbook treatment
7a.watch:
• Classification separates by settling velocity, not by size alone: a small dense grain can report with a large light one. For example (Stokes, water at 20 degrees C), a 50 micrometre galena grain settles with a quartz grain of about 98 micrometres.
  • Stokes' law holds only for small Reynolds numbers (fine particles, below roughly 50 to 100 micrometres in water); coarser particles pass through an intermediate range into the turbulent (Newton) regime, reached at a few millimetres.

7b.fix:
• Slide 79 writes sodium ethyl xanthate as \mathrm{C_2H_5OS_2Na}; the formula is \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2Na} (the \mathrm{CS_2} carbon is missing), and the anion is \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2^-}.
  • Slide 83 calls \mathrm{Cu_2S} "chalcopyrite"; \mathrm{Cu_2S} is chalcocite (the course book says chalcocite), and chalcopyrite is \mathrm{CuFeS_2}. The complex printed as "Cu(CN)" is the cuprocyanide ion, for example \mathrm{[Cu(CN)_2]^-}.
7b.html:
Froth flotation separates minerals by surface wettability: air bubbles pass through a pulp (about one third solids), hydrophobic particles attach to them and rise into a froth that is skimmed off, and hydrophilic particles stay in the pulp. Most minerals are ionically or covalently bonded and naturally hydrophilic, so reagents must create and control the difference.

1. Collectors. Heteropolar organic surfactants: a polar group that adsorbs on the chosen mineral and a non-polar hydrocarbon chain that faces the water. The water then "sees" a hydrocarbon film, so the mineral becomes hydrophobic and sticks to bubbles. Example: sodium ethyl xanthate, \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2Na}, dissociates to \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2^-} and \mathrm{Na^+}; the -\mathrm{S^-} end bonds to \mathrm{Pb^{2+}} or \mathrm{Cu^{+}} at a sulphide surface (100-750 g/t). Collectors are anionic (xanthates, dithiophosphates) or cationic (amines). Role: the main reagent of selective flotation.

2. Frothers. Heteropolar surface-active organics (pine oil, cresylic acid; 50-300 g/t) that adsorb at the air-water interface, polar group in the water and chain in the air, and lower the surface tension. Role: fine, stable bubbles and a froth that holds the mineral until it is skimmed, yet breaks down afterwards; if bubbles burst, the load falls back. Ideally they do not act on the mineral.

3. Activators. They make a surface more amenable to the collector (a supporting role). Sphalerite floats poorly with xanthate because zinc xanthate is fairly soluble; \mathrm{CuSO_4} (300-500 g/t) puts copper into the surface,

\mathrm{ZnS(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow CuS(s) + Zn^{2+}(aq)}

and xanthate then adsorbs strongly, so sphalerite floats.

4. Depressors (depressants). The opposite role: they make a surface inactive to the collector, so that mineral stays in the pulp. With galena and chalcocite (\mathrm{Cu_2S}), NaCN (up to 1300 g/t) forms a stable cuprocyanide complex at the copper-mineral surface, for example \mathrm{Cu^+ + 2CN^- \rightarrow [Cu(CN)_2]^-}, while the lead cyanide complex is unstable; xanthate then adsorbs only on galena, which floats. Lime at pH about 11.5 depresses pyrite.

5. Conditioners (pH regulators). Lime (CaO, 1-2 kg/t; cheaper and gives a higher pH) and soda ash (\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}, 400-800 g/t). Each mineral has a critical pH for a given collector concentration, above which it does not float, so pH sets selectivity. They also precipitate \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} and \mathrm{Pb^{2+}} that would cause unwanted activation, prevent collector hydrolysis at low pH and reduce corrosion. The pulp is conditioned (agitated with the reagents) for 10-20 min before the cells.

In sequence (Pb-Zn ore): float galena with xanthate; then raise the pH to 11.5 to depress pyrite, activate sphalerite with \mathrm{CuSO_4} and float it.
pts: States that flotation separates by wettability (hydrophobic particles attach to bubbles and float) and that most minerals are naturally hydrophilic, so reagents are needed
Collector: heteropolar organic reagent whose polar group adsorbs on the mineral and whose non-polar chain faces the water, making the mineral hydrophobic
Collector example: xanthate dissociates and its -\mathrm{S^-} bonds to the cations of a sulphide surface (or gives a dose, 100-750 g/t)
Names collector types: anionic and cationic (or ionising and non-ionising)
Frother: surface-active reagent that adsorbs at the air-water interface and lowers the surface tension, with an example (pine oil, cresylic acid)
Frother role: stable bubbles and froth that carry the mineral to the surface without breaking, but not so stable that the froth cannot be handled
Activator: makes the surface amenable to the collector, with the \mathrm{CuSO_4} on sphalerite example (\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} replaces \mathrm{Zn^{2+}})
Depressor: makes the surface inactive to the collector, with the NaCN example (stable copper cyanide complex, so galena floats and the copper mineral stays) or lime on pyrite
Conditioner: pH regulator (lime, soda ash), critical pH, plus one extra function (precipitates heavy-metal ions, stops collector hydrolysis, cuts corrosion)
Conditioning period: the pulp is agitated with reagents for 10-20 min before flotation
Shows the reagents working together, for example the Pb-Zn sequence (galena first, then pyrite depressed at pH 11.5 and sphalerite activated)

7b.watch:
• "Depressor" and "depressant" are the same reagent; "conditioner" in the course table means the pH regulators lime and soda ash, while "conditioning" is the agitation period.
  • The frother acts at the air-water surface, the collector at the mineral-water surface; swapping these is the commonest error.
  • Do not say NaCN depresses galena: in the course example it depresses the copper sulphide and galena floats.

8a.html:
Minerals with a wide range of electrical conductivity are separated by electrostatic (high-tension) separation, which exploits the difference in conductivity between minerals.

Principle. All particles are given a surface charge, then brought against an earthed surface. A conductor loses its charge to earth at once (or takes an induced charge) and is free to leave the surface. A non-conductor keeps its charge and is held to the earthed surface by its image force. The two then follow different paths.

Charging methods: ion bombardment from a corona discharge, conductive induction near a charged electrode, and contact (triboelectric) charging.

Feed: dry (surface moisture makes every particle conduct), usually heated, and closely sized fine sand (roughly below 1 mm).

High-tension roll separator.

  1. Dry feed falls from a hopper onto the top of a rotating, earthed metal roll.
  2. The roll carries the particles past an ionising (corona) electrode, a fine wire at high voltage (tens of kV), which sprays ions so that every particle is charged.
  3. Conductors pass their charge to the earthed roll quickly. Gravity and the centrifugal force throw them off the roll, and a static (non-ionising) electrode beyond it attracts them by induction and lifts them further out, into the conductors bin.
  4. Non-conductors keep their charge and are pinned to the roll by the image force. They are carried round underneath and removed by a brush into the non-conductors bin.
  5. Particles of intermediate conductivity, and locked particles, fall between them as middlings; adjustable splitters set the cuts, and middlings are re-treated in further stages.

Applications: heavy mineral beach sands, where rutile and ilmenite (conductors) are separated from zircon and monazite (non-conductors); also cleaning of iron ore and cassiterite concentrates.
pts: Names electrostatic (high-tension) separation and states the principle: conductors lose their charge to an earthed surface, non-conductors keep it
Charging methods: corona (ion bombardment), induction, contact
Feed must be dry, heated and closely sized fine
Neat labelled sketch: hopper, earthed rotating roll, corona electrode, static electrode, brush, splitters, three products
The corona electrode at high voltage charges all particles on the roll
Conductors discharge to the earthed roll and are thrown off (centrifugal force, attraction of the static electrode) into the conductors bin
Non-conductors stay charged, are pinned to the roll by the image force and are brushed off underneath
Middlings fall between; splitters adjustable; middlings re-treated
An application, for example rutile and ilmenite (conductors) from zircon and monazite (non-conductors)
8a.sketch:
• Feed hopper above an earthed, rotating roll, with the direction of rotation.
  • Ionising (corona) wire electrode and the static electrode beside the roll.
  • Trajectory of conductors away from the roll; non-conductors on the roll surface to the brush.
  • Splitters and three bins: conductors, middlings, non-conductors.
8a.src: Book Ch 1 reading, p 27; Particle selection reading 4 (end-of-chapter questions), p 14; Standard textbook treatment
8a.watch:
• The course slides do not cover electrical separation; this answer follows the standard ore-dressing texts, hence medium confidence.
  • The roll is earthed and the corona wire is at high voltage; drawing the roll as the charged electrode reverses the mechanism.
  • Moisture is the main enemy: a damp feed makes every particle behave as a conductor.

8b.html:
Why drying is expensive

Thickening is the cheapest dewatering method (40-50 % water left), filtration is dearer (about 10 %), drying is the dearest (zero).

  1. Thickening and filtration remove water as a liquid, mechanically: gravity settling (slow rakes, almost no power or attendance, so the cost is mainly capital) and a pressure difference across a filter cloth. No phase change.
  2. Drying must convert the water to vapour: heat raises the water to its boiling point and supplies the large latent heat of evaporation (2257 kJ/kg at 100 C), about 2.57 MJ per kg of water from 25 C, all from fuel.
  3. Heat is also lost to the solids and the hot exit gas, and the gas raises dust.

Per tonne of dry solids, a 10 % filter cake holds 111 kg of water (about 0.29 GJ to evaporate); a 45 % thickener underflow holds 818 kg (about 2.1 GJ). So the cheap methods remove most water, and drying only the last part that smelting and shipping require.

Drying in a rotary cylindrical drier

  1. Shell: sheet-steel cylinder, 5-30 m long, 0.9-3.0 m in diameter, sloping 3-5 degrees, on rollers, turned at 1.5-2 rpm by a drive gear.
  2. Wet material is fed continuously at the raised end.
  3. Lifting flights (shelves) turn the material over and over through the gas and stop it sticking; with the slope it moves toward the discharge end.
  4. Hot gases (750-1000 C) from burning fuel enter at the discharge end and flow counter-current, leaving cool and moist at the feed end.
  5. The hottest, driest gas meets the nearly dry solids, so the last traces of moisture are removed efficiently, and heat use is good.
  6. Dry solids leave continuously at the lower end.
pts: Gives the comparison: thickening cheapest (40-50 % water), filtration more expensive (about 10 %), drying most expensive (zero water)
Thickening and filtration remove liquid water mechanically (gravity, pressure difference) with little energy; thickening cost is mainly capital
Drying must evaporate the water: sensible heat plus the large latent heat of evaporation (about 2260 kJ/kg), supplied by fuel
Extra heat losses (hot exit gas, heating the solids) or dust formation
Concludes that cheap mechanical dewatering is done first and drying removes only the last water, which later steps require (or a worked energy figure)
Construction: steel cylinder 5-30 m long, 0.9-3.0 m diameter, slope 3-5 degrees, on rollers, 1.5-2 rpm
Lifting flights or shelves turn the material over through the gas and stop it sticking; it moves toward the discharge end
Wet feed charged continuously at the raised end; dry product leaves at the lower end
Hot gases (750-1000 C) flow counter-current, so the hottest, driest gas removes the last traces of moisture efficiently
Moist, cooled gas leaves at the feed end
8b.sketch:
• Inclined cylinder with feed at the raised end and dry solids out at the lower end.
  • Hot gas in at the discharge end, moist gas out at the feed end (arrows opposite to the solids).
  • Riding rings on rollers and the drive (girth) gear.
  • Lifting flights inside (a cross-section helps).
8b.src: Particle selection (supersedes the 72-slide version), slides 89-90, 92-97; Particle selection reading 4 (end-of-chapter questions), pp 9-13
8b.watch:
• No sketch is asked, so none is credited; a quick sketch is still the fastest way to show the counter-current flows.
  • Do not say thickening "evaporates" anything: thickening and filtration leave the water liquid, which is why they are cheap.
  • The drawing on slides 96-97 is a steam-heated air drier (steam coils and condensate at the air inlet), while the slide text gives combustion gases at 750-1000 C; steam-heated air is far cooler. Both are counter-current, and either heating method describes the operation.
  • The heat figures assume the water is heated from 25 C and evaporated; real driers need more because of exit-gas and shell losses.
